attempt.explanation: The diagnosis reads the three CSV copies with csv.DictReader (utf-8-sig, newline=''), keys rows by the literal invoice_id string, and compares the last good backup against the checkpoint taken right after the bad import. Only the price column differs between those two versions, matching the reported 100x multiplication, so price is the affected field. For each record present in all three versions whose price changed between backup and checkpoint, one cell is proposed to revert it; the 7 post-incident records and any record absent today are excluded, later payment_status edits are preserved, and no file is modified.

proposal.summary: The bad import multiplied the price column by 100 for all 120 records that existed at the time; comparing the last good backup with the checkpoint right after the import confirmed price changed on every record while customer, payment_status and created_on did not change during the incident. The proposed cells revert price on records present in all three versions, excluding the 7 records created after the incident and any record missing today. Records whose price was edited again after the incident are still included because the controller independently protects overlaps. Later payment_status updates are left untouched, and no files were modified.

attempts.explanation: The program repairs only the individually approved cells. For CSV, it reads the current file with csv.DictReader (utf-8-sig, newline='') so every value stays an exact string — leading zeros, decimals, whitespace, commas, Unicode, newlines and empty strings are preserved and nothing is converted. It builds a lookup of backup records by primary key, then for each entry in scope.cells it finds the current row with that same key and copies just that one column's value from the backup. It never combines the keys and columns summaries into a Cartesian product. All current rows are written back in their original order with the original fieldnames using csv.DictWriter (utf-8, newline=''), so every unapproved cell, key and column name is untouched. For SQLite, the current database is copied to the output first (schema and counters preserved), the backup is opened read-only/immutable, and each approved cell is applied with a parameterized UPDATE using quoted identifiers; the output connection is committed and closed before returning. No network, printing, or wholesale copying of the backup occurs.
